blocks.text: Once upon a time in Ireland, there was a chief called Allil. One day, while he was unguarded, a band of raiders landed from their ships, and they killed him, and burned the church where he had hidden.

Not long afterwards, Allil's wife had a baby boy, and she called him Maildun. She was afraid for him, so she gave him to her best friend, the queen, to bring up. The queen pretended he was her own child, and he grew up with her three sons in the king's palace. He was a lovely child, and he grew into a fine young man, better than anyone at running and jumping, at rowing and racing, and at chess.
One day, a jealous boy said, "It's a shame that we always lose to someone when nobody even knows who his father and mother are!"

Maildun stopped playing at once. Until that moment he had thought the king and queen were his parents. He went to the queen. "If you are not my mother," he said, "I won't eat or drink until you tell me who my parents are."
"Am I not a mother to you?" said the queen. "Is there any mother in the land who loves her son more?"
"That's true," said Maildun. "But please tell me."

So the queen took him to his real mother, and she told him who his father had been. Maildun went to live among his father's people, and his three foster brothers went with him. And then he learned how his father had died. "The raiders who killed him are still sailing the sea in their ships," someone told him.

So Maildun decided to find them. He went to a wise druid for advice about building a boat. The druid told him on which day to start building it, and on which day to set sail. "And you must take exactly sixty men with you," he said. "No more, and no less."

So Maildun built a big boat out of three layers of hide, called a curragh, and chose sixty men to sail with him, among them his two best friends, Germane and Diuran. And on the right day they set out to sea.
But they had only gone a little way when they saw his three foster brothers running down to the shore. "Come back and take us with you!" they shouted.
"We can't," Maildun called back. "We have exactly the number we need."
"Then we'll swim after you until we drown!" said his brothers. And they jumped into the sea and swam after the boat. Maildun could not let them drown, so he turned back and took them on board.

They sailed for a day and a night and another day. At midnight they came to two small islands, and they heard voices from a great house, and one man boasting: "I'm the one who killed Allil and burned the church over his head, and no one has ever dared to punish me!"
"Heaven has brought us here!" said Germane and Diuran. But at that very moment a great storm blew up, and swept them far out into the endless ocean, until they had no idea where they were.

"This has happened because we broke the druid's rule," said Maildun. "Let's put down our oars and let the boat go wherever God sends it." And so began their voyage among the islands of the Western Sea, which lasted three years and seven months.
The first island they found was swarming with ants, each as big as a young horse. They looked very hungry, so the sailors turned the boat round and sailed quickly away.

On another island, a monster like a horse with the legs of a dog and sharp blue claws danced about on the beach, delighted to see them, for it meant to eat them all. "He seems very glad we've come," said Maildun. "Let's go somewhere else." And when the monster saw them leaving, it threw stones at them in a rage.

Next they came to an island with a hill all round it, and a single apple tree in the middle. Its branches were so long and thin that they grew right over the hill and down to the sea. Maildun caught hold of one branch and held it, letting it slide through his hand, while they sailed round the island for three days and three nights. At the very end of the branch he found seven apples. And each apple gave them all food and drink for forty days and forty nights.

On another island there was a huge beast with thick rough skin. Every day it ran round the island as fast as the wind. Then it stood on a flat rock and turned round and round inside its own skin, while the skin stayed still. Then it kept its body still and turned its skin round and round instead, like a mill wheel. The sailors decided not to land there. The beast ran down to the beach and threw a stone at them so hard that it went straight through Maildun's shield.

Then, after a long, hungry time, they came to an island full of trees with golden apples. Under the trees lived herds of animals like pigs, glowing bright red, because they were full of fire. All day long they kicked the trees to shake down the apples and ate them, and at sunset they went into caves underground. Then flocks of birds flew in from the sea and ate the apples all night. "If the birds can do it, so can we," said Maildun. So when night came, the sailors landed, though the ground was hot under their feet from the fiery animals sleeping below, and they picked as many apples as their boat would hold.

When the apples ran out, they came to an island with a white palace. Inside, there was nobody but a little cat, jumping from the top of one marble pillar to another. Around the walls hung gold and silver brooches, golden collars, and swords with golden hilts. A feast was laid out on the tables.
"Is this food for us?" Maildun asked the cat. The cat looked at him for a moment, and then went back to its jumping. So they sat down and ate, and slept on the soft couches.
As they were leaving, Maildun's eldest foster brother said, "Shall I take one of those golden collars?"
"No!" said Maildun. "Take nothing. Somebody must be guarding this place."

But his brother took one anyway. And the little cat leaped after him like a flaming arrow, and in a flash he was turned to ashes. Maildun put the collar back, and spoke gently to the cat. Then they scattered his brother's ashes on the sea and sailed on, very sad.

On one island, a wall of brass ran down the middle. On one side were black sheep, and on the other side were white ones. A big man was throwing sheep over the wall, and whenever a white sheep landed among the black ones, it turned black, and whenever a black sheep landed among the white ones, it turned white. The sailors threw a black stick onto the white side, and it turned white at once. "Good thing we didn't land," said Maildun. "We would have changed colour too!"
On another island, Germane and Diuran saw a herd of animals as big as oxen, with a giant looking after them. Germane banged his spear on his shield to make them get up.
"Why are you frightening my poor little calves?" boomed the giant.
"If those are the calves," said Germane, "where are their mothers?"
"Over on that mountain," said the giant. Germane and Diuran didn't wait to hear any more. They ran back to the boat, and they all sailed away.

Then they came to an island where everybody was dressed in black, and walked about weeping and wringing their hands. Maildun's second foster brother went ashore to look, and at once he began to weep and wring his hands too, and they could never find him again among all the weeping people. So they had to sail away without him.

They sailed over a sea as clear as green crystal, where they could see the shining sand at the bottom. Then they sailed over a sea so thin and clear that it looked like a cloud, and far below them they could see a whole country, with houses and woods and herds of cattle.

They came to a great silver pillar standing all alone in the sea, so tall they could not see the top. A silver net hung down from it, with holes so big that their boat sailed right through one of them. Diuran cut a piece off the net with his spear. "So that people will believe our story," he said. "And I will lay it on the altar at Armagh, if I ever get home." And from somewhere high up on the pillar they heard a voice speaking, loud and clear and glad, in a language they did not know.

They came to an island ruled by a beautiful queen. She gave them a feast and soft beds. "Stay here," she said. "You will never grow old or ill, and you will always be happy." So they stayed for three months. But the men began to miss home, and one day, while the queen was away, they slipped out to sea. The queen came riding back and saw them. She threw a ball of thread after the boat, and Maildun caught it, and it stuck to his hand. And the queen pulled the thread, and drew the boat back to shore.

Every time they tried to escape, the same thing happened. After nine months, the men said, "Maildun loves the queen. That's why he always catches the ball." So the next time, someone else caught it. It stuck to his hand too. But Diuran drew his sword and cut him free, and the ball fell into the sea, and they rowed away, while the queen and her maidens wept on the shore.

On another island, they met a very old holy man, one of the companions of Saint Brendan, who had sailed out into the ocean long ago. While they were there, an enormous bird came flying over the sea, as big as a cloud, holding a branch heavy with red fruit. It was very old, and its feathers were thin and worn. The sailors were frightened, but the bird took no notice of them. Then two younger birds came and spent three days picking out its old feathers and smoothing its new ones, and the old bird bathed in the lake. And when it rose up into the air again, it was young and strong and glossy, and it flew away with the others. Diuran jumped into the lake too, and for the rest of his life he never lost a tooth or had a grey hair.

On the next island, everyone was playing games and laughing, laughing, laughing. Maildun's third foster brother went ashore, and at once he started playing and laughing with them, as if he had always lived there. He never came back to the boat. So now all three of Maildun's foster brothers were gone.

At last they met an old hermit, covered all over in long white hair, living alone on a rock in the sea. He told them that long ago he had been a wicked man, who had stolen treasure from a church. But a holy man had appeared to him on the waves and made him throw all his stolen treasure into the sea, and he had come to live on this rock, to pray and be sorry. For seven years an otter had brought him a salmon every day, and another otter had brought him firewood to cook it.

"You will all get home safely," the hermit told them. "And Maildun, on the way you will find the man who killed your father. But you must not harm him. God has forgiven you for many things and brought you safely through many dangers. So you must forgive your enemy too."

Soon afterwards they came to a green island, and while they were there, a falcon flew past. "Look!" cried two of the sailors. "That falcon looks just like the falcons at home in Ireland!" "Watch which way it goes," said Maildun. It flew to the south-east, and they followed it. And at evening they came to the very island where their voyage had begun, where the man who had killed Maildun's father lived.
They crept up to the house and listened. The people inside were having supper. "What would we do if Maildun came here now?" one of them asked.
"He was drowned long ago," said another.

Then Maildun heard the voice of the chief of the house, the man who had killed his father. "If Maildun came now," he said, "after all his hardships, I would give him a warm welcome, even though we were enemies once."

So Maildun knocked on the door. "It's me, Maildun," he said, "home safe from all my wanderings." And the chief opened the door, and welcomed them in, and gave them new clothes and a great feast. And Maildun forgave him, as the hermit had told him to.

They told everyone about all the wonders they had seen. Then Maildun went home to his own people. And Diuran laid his piece of silver from the great net on the altar at Armagh, just as he had promised.
A simplified retelling of P. W. Joyce's “The Voyage of Maildun” in Old Celtic Romances (1879). The original is listed under Other versions. Joyce spells his name Maildun; in Irish it is Máel Dúin.
